soil-bio-079.title: Lumbricus terrestris, the nightcrawler that remakes forest soils
soil-bio-079.text: The common earthworm, lob worm or nightcrawler is Lumbricus terrestris, a large, reddish worm thought to be native to Western Europe and now spread around the world. It is generally 110–200 millimeters long and 7–10 millimeters across, with around 120–170 segments. Through much of Europe it is the largest naturally occurring earthworm. A deep-burrowing anecic worm, it digs vertical burrows, pulls surface litter down into the mineral soil and leaves casts of mixed organic and mineral material on the surface. Where it has invaded {{ref:soil-class-138}}, it has erased their banded profile of litter, pale E and colored B horizons. Thin litter and a dark, worm-mixed Ap horizon over the B are left behind. In the north central United States it is invasive. It thrives in fence rows and woodlots and reduces the regrowth of native plants and trees, though it fares poorly in tilled fields.

soil-bio-012.title: Actinomycetes, the bacteria once mistaken for fungi
soil-bio-012.text: The sweet, earthy smell of healthy soil comes from the volatile compounds of actinomycetes. These are soil bacteria of the phylum Actinomycetota, formerly Actinobacteria. They are Gram-positive and rich in guanine and cytosine, and many grow branching, fungus-like threads called mycelia. The order name Actinomycetales recalls that they were long thought to be fungi. Fungi do similar work, but actinomycetes are much smaller and likely fill a different niche. They decompose the remains of dead organisms so plants can take up the nutrients anew. They also help build stable dark soil matter by breaking down cellulose, tough woody compounds and the chitin of arthropods. The phylum is one of the dominant bacterial groups and includes Streptomyces, one of the largest bacterial genera. Streptomyces and its relatives are major contributors to the biological buffering of soils. Some, such as Frankia, live with plant roots, fixing nitrogen in exchange for some of the plant's sugars. They need plenty of air and a pH between 6.0 and 7.5, but tolerate dry conditions better than most bacteria and fungi. They also stock the medicine cabinet. They yield many antibiotics, among them streptomycin, neomycin, erythromycin and tetracycline, plus farm compounds such as insecticides, herbicides, fungicides and plant growth promoters.

soil-bio-043.title: How a few earthworm species hitched rides around the world
soil-bio-043.text: Of around 7,000 earthworm species, only about 150 are widely distributed. These are the peregrine or cosmopolitan earthworms, carried by people into regions where they are not native. In the United States and Canada, 70 of the 308 earthworm taxa, or 23%, are introduced species. Humans have spread surface-dwelling earthworms into many new regions, where they speed up carbon cycling. The effects reach deep into the soil profile. In {{ref:soil-class-138}}, invading worms can erase the banded layers, mixing the organic, E and upper B horizons into a single dark Ap horizon.

soil-bio-044.title: Vermicomposting: putting worms to work on waste
soil-bio-044.text: Vermicomposting feeds organic waste to earthworms and collects what comes out the other end. It usually relies on the brandling worms Eisenia fetida or Eisenia andrei, which live in manure heaps rather than soil. In the tropics, the African nightcrawler and the Indian blue are used. The end product is {{ref:soil-fert-039}}, also called worm castings. Worms fed partly composted material excrete castings that make nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus and magnesium available to plants. Added to soil, ideally spread on the surface, this humified material improves moisture and nutrient availability and benefits soil microbes.

soil-bio-004.title: Ecosystem engineers, the builders of soil habitat
soil-bio-004.text: Some species matter less for who eats them than for what they build. Ecosystem engineers are species that create, significantly modify, maintain or destroy a habitat. In soil they are chiefly burrowing animals such as earthworms, ants and termites, along with fungi. Engineers are defined by how they modify resources for other organisms, not by being eaten, which sets them apart from keystone species. Allogenic engineers change materials mechanically, as burrowers do. Autogenic engineers create habitat with their own bodies, as Sphagnum moss builds {{ref:soil-water-136}}. Earthworms, ants and termites mix the soil as they burrow. They strongly affect soil formation and the fate of soil organic matter while building crumbly, granular structure. Ant and termite nests enrich soil in carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus and mix particles from different depths. Moles, gophers and prairie dogs turn soil, spread fungi that partner with roots, and open corridors used by arthropods, birds, small mammals and reptiles. Fungi are engineers too. By linking distant patches and moving nutrients between them, even shifting carbon between trees, they control nutrient cycles. Where earthworms do little, potworms take on the role, digging galleries in which they leave their feces. Earthworms are particularly sensitive to many contaminants, and losing such engineers dramatically changes the organic layers at the soil surface. Not everyone likes the term. Some ecologists call it a buzzword, arguing that it implies intent or that every species would qualify.

soil-bio-047.title: Bioturbation: how burrowers stir the earth
soil-bio-047.text: In the 1800s Darwin watched a field slowly swallow a layer of chalk. Spread on the surface, the chalk lay 18 centimeters deep after 30 years, a burial rate of 6 millimeters per year that he credited to earthworms. That began the formal study of bioturbation: the reworking of soils and sediments by animals or plants, through burrowing and the swallowing and excreting of grains. Walruses, salmon and pocket gophers are conspicuous bioturbators, but small invertebrates such as earthworms, polychaete worms, shrimps and midge larvae dominate. Bioturbation differs from bioirrigation, the mixing of water and dissolved substances in sediments, which is one of its effects. Burrowers carry oxygen into oxygen-poor layers, changing how microbes live and speeding the breakdown of soil organic matter. Their burrows shelter other species. The process profoundly affects the environment and is thought to be a primary driver of biodiversity. Nathaniel Shaler added ants and trees to the story in 1891. Rudolf Richter coined the term in 1952, and it has been widely used in soil science and geomorphology, the study of landforms, since the 1980s. The process itself is far older. Since it began around 539 million years ago it has changed ocean chemistry, and it is thought to have been a co-factor of the Cambrian Explosion. Pollution can run it backward. When pollution harms earthworms, termites and ants, bioturbation falls and the {{ref:soil-bio-095}} shifts toward mor.

soil-bio-018.title: Farming with microbes: promise and pitfalls
soil-bio-018.text: Healthy soil life can supply crops with nutrients such as nitrogen and protect them against pests and diseases, while reducing the need for water and other inputs. Using and managing soil microorganisms toward those ends is the agricultural use of soil microbes. The partnership is fragile. Fertilizer and pesticide used without offsetting their effects can destroy the rhizobiome, the microbial ecosystem around roots. Excess fertilizer, phosphorus above a threshold in particular, can suppress the fungi that partner with roots and turn symbiotic bacteria into competitors. Almost all registered microbial products are biopesticides, now about 10% of the global pesticide market. Long-marketed examples include Trichoderma fungi, which suppress disease-causing fungi, and the caterpillar killer Bacillus thuringiensis. The field is hard going. Many strains that look promising in the lab fail outdoors because of soil, climate and ecosystem effects. Introduced populations can fade, as Bacillus subtilis does when it lacks a niche it can defend. Using several collaborating strains helps. Rules demanding safety evidence have even led many products to call themselves 'biostimulants' rather than 'biopesticides'.

soil-bio-070.title: Microbial inoculants: bottled helpers for crops
soil-bio-070.text: An estimated 836 million USD is spent on microbial inoculants each year. These farm amendments, also called soil inoculants or bioinoculants, use beneficial microbes that live around or inside roots to promote plant health. Many of the microbes form mutually beneficial partnerships with the crop. Besides improving nutrition, they can promote growth by stimulating the plant's hormone production. Bacterial inoculants, called plant growth promoting {{ref:soil-bio-154}}, include nitrogen fixers and phosphate solubilisers. The most commonly applied is Rhizobium, which fixes nitrogen in the root nodules of legumes. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi are used to supply phosphorus. In one greenhouse with reduced fertilization, these fungi plus root bacteria gave tomato yields at 70% fertility that matched those at 100%. Inoculants can also induce systemic acquired resistance, a whole-plant defense, shown so far against powdery mildew, take-all, leaf spot and root rot. Mixing strains raises nutrient uptake from soil and fertilizer. Several strains together even raise the activity of the nitrogen-fixing enzyme when only one of them fixes nitrogen. Inoculants often change the soil's existing microbial community. Results so far are mixed. Research in 2024 suggests as few as one in nine commercial products are beneficial, and with commercial products root colonization by these fungi was under 10%. Large-scale application is not yet economically viable, so inoculants are not widely used in industrial agriculture.

soil-bio-048.title: Gophers, worms and fallen trees: how soil gets stirred
soil-bio-048.text: Pocket gophers may produce soil on a scale equal to non-living processes. Bioturbation in soils is the mixing and moving of soil by burrowing animals and plant roots. It matters for soil production, burial, soil organic matter content and the movement of soil downslope. Plants and animals disturb the upper soil and bring weathered rock, saprolite, up from depth to the surface. Gopher mounds carry little-weathered rock up, speeding soil formation, and are easily eroded downslope. The mounds also bury plants, which decay into nutrient hotspots. Burrows, even when backfilled, lower soil density. Burrows of earthworms and small mammals carry air and water. They change porosity, nutrient content and how particle sizes are spread with depth. Trees play their part. Roots add soil organic matter and leave voids when they rot, and uprooted trees throw up mounds and can turn sections of soil upside down. Burrowers that eat dead matter build the organic-rich topsoil called the soil biomantle, and so help form soil horizons.

soil-bio-077.title: Sorting bacteria by how they eat and breathe
soil-bio-077.text: Bacteria can be sorted by three questions: where their energy comes from, which electron donors they use and where they get their carbon. Electrons are the currency of {{ref:soil-chem-113}}. Phototrophs get their energy from light by photosynthesis, while chemotrophs get it by oxidizing chemical compounds. Bacteria that take electrons from inorganic compounds such as hydrogen, carbon monoxide or ammonia are covered in {{ref:soil-bio-056}}; those that use organic compounds are organotrophs. Heterotrophs take their carbon from organic compounds, while autotrophs such as cyanobacteria and some purple bacteria fix carbon dioxide. Aerobes use oxygen as the final electron acceptor, and anaerobes use nitrate, sulfate or carbon dioxide. Facultative anaerobes switch between fermentation and different acceptors as conditions change.

soil-bio-056.title: Lithotrophs, the microbes that eat rock
soil-bio-056.text: Life's last universal common ancestor is thought to have been a chemolithotroph, a microbe living on the chemical energy of inorganic substances. A lithotroph is any organism that takes the electrons it needs from an inorganic substance, usually of mineral origin, rather than from organic compounds. It uses them to build cells or make energy. The name joins the Greek lithos, rock, and troph, consumer: lithotrophs are 'eaters of rock'. Lwoff and collaborators suggested the term in 1946. The opposite strategy is the organotroph, which gets its electrons by breaking down organic compounds. In the broad sense, lithotrophs include light-using photolithotrophs such as plants. Chemolithotrophs, though, are exclusively microorganisms, all in the domains Bacteria and Archaea. Lithoautotrophs take their carbon from carbon dioxide in the air, as plants do. Lithoheterotrophs cannot fix carbon dioxide and must consume organic compounds; only a few bacteria are fully lithoheterotrophic. Many lithotrophs are mixotrophs, topping up the carbon they fix with organic material. They live in the deep subsurface, soils, mines and endolith communities inside rock. There they take part in soil formation and the cycling of carbon, nitrogen and other elements. In the cycling of iron they can use it both ways: as an electron donor, turning Fe(II) into Fe(III), or as an electron acceptor, turning Fe(III) into Fe(II).

soil-bio-057.title: Chemolithotrophy: making a living from minerals in the dark
soil-bio-057.text: Some microbes build living matter in total darkness, from nothing but minerals and gases. {{ref:soil-hist-013}} first characterized their metabolism, chemolithotrophy. In 1887, working with the bacterium Beggiatoa, he discovered the first known form of lithotrophy. In chemolithotrophy a cell gets its energy by oxidizing reduced inorganic compounds such as ammonia, sulfur, ferrous iron or hydrogen. The oxidation is coupled to making ATP, the cell's energy carrier. Electrons taken from the inorganic donor pass into respiratory chains that make ATP. Most chemolithotrophs also fix carbon dioxide, usually through the Calvin cycle, an energetically expensive pathway. The group includes sulfur oxidizers, iron oxidizers, hydrogen oxidizers and the bacteria that turn ammonia into nitrite and nitrite into nitrate. Oxygen is the usual electron acceptor in the best-documented forms. Nitrate and other acceptors are also used, and the list of chemolithotrophs that live without oxygen is growing. Energy yields depend on the fuel. Oxidizing hydrogen sulfide to sulfur gives 50 kcal/mol (210 kJ/mol), while oxidizing sulfur to sulfate gives 150 kcal/mol (627 kJ/mol). On low-energy fuels such as ferrous iron, cells must process large amounts of material for a little energy, which keeps them from thriving in many places. Because this kind of chemosynthesis needs no sunlight, chemolithotrophs can build living material in the dark. Some thrive above 110 degrees Celsius or below pH 2.

soil-bio-009.title: What acid, salt and the plow do to soil life
soil-bio-009.text: In Dutch soils below pH 5, biodiversity fell as pH fell, in grasslands and heathlands alike. Threats to soil biodiversity are soil changes that reduce the variety of soil life, such as acidification, salinization, sodicity, structure decline and erosion. Many are driven by how soil is managed. Acidification cuts the numbers of most large soil animals, earthworms included. It harms the survival of rhizobium bacteria and may slow decay and the capture of nitrogen from the air. Salt works differently. At low salinity microbes are active and soil respiration is high; as salinity rises, microbes have less available water and respire less. Prolonged high sodium leaves soil cement-like, holding and passing less water and breaking down soil organic matter more slowly. Erosion strips topsoil, soil organic matter and nutrients and breaks down structure, making it a major threat. Constant {{ref:soil-agri-095}} redistributes soil organic matter, degrading structure and altering populations of earthworms and other organisms. Even a common fertilizer can harm. Chloride from potassium chloride raises salinity and is biocidal, harming the growth, survival and reproduction of soil organisms, including the bacteria that make nitrate.

soil-bio-084.title: Thatch, the spongy mat that builds up under lawns
soil-bio-084.text: In lawn care, thatch is a layer of plant material that builds up around the base of the grass plants. It mixes living and dead crowns, stolons, rhizomes and roots. About 25% of it is {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, which resists decay. Grass clippings add little, because soil microbes break them down easily. Thatch builds up when acid soils cannot support enough decomposers, or when insecticides cut earthworm activity and so bioturbation. Excess nitrogen fertilizer adds to it by spurring growth and acidifying the soil. A thin layer insulates against swings in temperature and moisture. Too much causes root problems and mowing difficulties, and is removed with a dethatcher.

soil-bio-023.title: Macrofauna, the soil animals big enough to see
soil-bio-023.text: Earthworms, termites, ants, millipedes, woodlice, beetles, slugs and snails all belong to the soil macrofauna: soil and litter invertebrates between 2 mm and 2 cm long. Earthworms, termites, ants, some millipedes and some insect larvae make pore spaces and so change soil structure. Diets differ widely. Millipedes, woodlice and some earthworms eat leaf litter. Lower termites eat wood, while endogeic earthworms and higher termites eat dark, decayed soil organic matter. Centipedes and spiders hunt prey. Shredding plant remains speeds decay, and so does waking dormant bacteria in the soil the animals swallow. Researchers call this the 'Sleeping Beauty' paradigm, with the earthworm as 'Prince Charming'. Animals that eat dead matter need enzymes from gut microbes to digest wood or soil organic matter. In lower termites, partner flagellates help digest the tough fibers of wood. Food ground in earthworm gizzards or chewed by termites leaves pasty feces that harden into stable earthworm casts and termite mounds. Macrofauna are abundant in fertile soils and typical of the mull type of {{ref:soil-bio-095}}, with many feeding niches and more complex food webs. They need much calcium and nitrogen, so they depend on plants with fast-decaying litter. By speeding nutrient cycling, they favor such plants in return: a positive feedback between life above and below ground.

soil-bio-022.title: Mesofauna, the mites and jumpers of the pore spaces
soil-bio-022.text: Between 0.2 mm and 2 mm long, the soil mesofauna are mostly microarthropods such as mites and {{ref:soil-bio-085}}, plus potworms ({{ref:soil-bio-087}}). The springing kind breed fast and live in large populations. They are prey for predatory mites, pseudoscorpions and macrofauna, which makes them pivotal in soil food webs. Mesofauna feed on plant remains, microbes, lichens, spores, pollen and other animals. Their heavy consumption of litter and microbes gives them an important part in the cycling of carbon. They also eat and break down the feces of larger animals, such as earthworm casts. Microarthropods cannot reshape soil and must use the existing macropores, which makes them very sensitive to compaction. Potworms instead dig galleries. By eating fungal threads and spores, mesofauna help regulate fungal communities, including fungi that partner with roots, both spreading and severing them. Their community make-up reflects environmental differences, so mesofauna are good bioindicators of soil quality. Being sensitive to environmental hazards, they are likely to be harmed by climate change, land use change and farming intensification.

soil-bio-085.title: Springtails, the tiny jumpers that graze on fungi
soil-bio-085.text: Estimates reach 100,000 springtails in a single square meter of ground. Springtails, class Collembola, are tiny six-legged arthropods, no longer counted as insects, that live in moist soil and leaf litter almost everywhere on Earth. More than 9,000 species are known. They are omnivorous and free-living, and prefer moist conditions. Temperate deciduous woodland litter typically holds 30 to 40 species, and the tropics may exceed 100. Springtails do not break down dead matter directly. They speed its decay by fragmenting it and by controlling and spreading soil microbes. They mostly eat fungal threads and spores, but also plant material, pollen, animal remains and bacteria. Geosmin from Streptomyces attracts some species, which eat and spread its spores. Mesostigmatan mites and soil centipedes hunt them. Springtails escape by jumping with a spring-like organ, the furcula, though that is hard to do inside soil. Their communities change with depth, from canopy to litter to deeper horizons, and across landscapes with acidity, moisture and light. As a group they are highly sensitive to drying out. Unlike earthworms, they are very sensitive to herbicides. Folsomia candida is used in standardized toxicity and avoidance tests for soil pollution, and springtails serve as bioindicators of soil quality. On lawns they act as 'thatch busters', helping break down the thatch between the grass and the soil surface.

soil-bio-087.title: Potworms, the earthworms' small white cousins
soil-bio-087.text: Over 700 species of enchytraeids are described. They form a family of small, earthworm-like oligochaete worms, and the land-dwelling species, called potworms, live in highly organic soils. Most are whitish or transparent and a few millimeters long. They eat decaying plant and animal matter and its microbes, aiding decay and nutrient cycling. Like earthworms, they are ecosystem engineers, shaping soil structure by building aggregates of various sizes. They feed on earthworm casts and turn them into fluffy masses of their own feces. Those masses make up the bulk of the OH horizon in the moder type of {{ref:soil-bio-095}}. They are less sensitive than earthworms to farming intensification. So they replace earthworms in soils with heavy pesticide use and serve in standard ecotoxicity tests (ISO 16387).

soil-bio-017.title: Slime molds and myxobacteria, single cells that act as one
soil-bio-017.text: A slime mold makes complex decisions about food with no coordinating center at all. Slime molds and myxobacteria are soil microorganisms whose single cells band together. Slime molds, which are eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus, merge into syncytia: one vast cell with many nuclei. Myxobacteria, which are prokaryotes, gather into swarms. Both glide in a coordinated way while foraging, a behavior still largely unexplored. Both also form spores in fruiting bodies, which are often iridescent and conspicuous.

soil-bio-013.title: Soil algae, sunlight harvesters at the surface
soil-bio-013.text: Soil algae are photosynthetic microorganisms that live at or near the soil surface and make their own carbon compounds from light. Needing light, they spread wherever sunlight and moderate moisture reach, but not far below the surface. Deeper down, some live on given steady temperature and moisture, taking in ready-made carbon such as glucose. Soil algae divide into green Chlorophyceae and golden-brown diatoms, which owe their color to the carotenoid pigment fucoxanthin. One alga, Chlorella vulgaris, has been shown to promote plant growth together with bacteria around roots.

soil-bio-016.title: Phages, the viruses that prey on soil bacteria
soil-bio-016.text: Viruses that infect soil bacteria, called bacteriophages or phages, are among the most abundant yet least studied members of soil microbial communities. Their richness varies with season, soil moisture, location and plant growth, and rises with the number of bacteria. Soil phages follow three strategies. Lytic phages kill the host to release new virus particles. Lysogenic phages join the host's genome. Chronic phages release particles without killing it. By killing hosts, lytic phages affect how bacteria cycle carbon, nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus. Phages are also a major route by which genes move between bacteria. They can even open plants to disease: phage ΦGP100 kills Pseudomonas fluorescens, a bacterium that produces antifungal compounds.

soil-bio-014.title: Protozoa, the soil's single-celled grazers
soil-bio-014.text: Heterotrophic flagellates may occasionally number several million in a gram of soil. They are the smallest of the soil protozoa, single-celled eukaryotes grouped as flagellates, amoebae and ciliates. Most protozoa eat bacteria. Others eat bacteria and fungi, fungi alone, or particles of decayed plant and animal matter. Naked amoebae move through water-filled pores and films. Testate amoebae shelter in shells against drying out, and they serve as indicators of past climates. Ciliates, the largest, move by many short beating cilia.

soil-bio-015.title: The microbial loop: how predators free nutrients for roots
soil-bio-015.text: Farooq Azam, Tom Fenchel and others coined the term microbial loop in 1983 for the role of bacteria in marine carbon and nutrient cycles. It names the pathway by which bacteria take up dissolved organic carbon and pass it back up the food web. 'Microbial food web' is now often used instead. In soil, the loop concerns carbon and the nutrients freed when protozoa and nematodes eat bacteria fed by roots. It runs like this. Roots pushing into new soil prime resting bacteria, which naked amoebae then eat. That frees mineral nitrogen for root hairs to absorb. Predation by amoebae and free-living nematodes raises the rate at which nutrients are released, which in turn stimulates root growth. This loop is Clarholm's hypothesis, and it is hard to verify by experiment. Bacteria-eating protozoa release the nutrients locked in microbial bodies in a form plants can use. A related idea, the microbial carbon pump model, has plants add carbon through {{ref:soil-bio-142}} and litter. Microbes then either respire it to the atmosphere or store it in a stable pool as dead microbial biomass, called necromass. They transform plant carbon outside the cell with enzymes and inside it as their populations grow and die. The balance between pathways that release CO2 and those that build carbon sets how much carbon the soil keeps. Fresh plant carbon can also prime microbes to break down carbon already stored in soil organic matter faster than models expect. Much remains unknown. Most of the soil microbiome has never been cultivated, which leaves its part in carbon cycling uncertain and hampers climate models of carbon flux.

soil-bio-049.title: When burrowers scramble the archaeologist's layers
soil-bio-049.text: Archaeologists date finds relatively by stratigraphy: in a stack of deposits, the topmost layer is the youngest. Burrowing organisms break that rule. By moving material up, down and sideways, bioturbation blurs the order in which deposits were laid down, confusing the archaeological record and making relative dating harder. Archaeologists study it alongside geologists and biologists.
